title: Malai Kofta Ranks Among World's 10 Best Deep-Fried Dishes
excerpt: Taste Atlas has placed the creamy North Indian classic at No. 10 on its list of the 50 best deep-fried dishes in the world, with Chicken 65 and papdi chaat also making the cut.
body:
• Taste Atlas has ranked malai kofta the 10th best deep-fried dish in the world on its list of the 50 best, placing the North Indian classic alongside heavyweights from South Korea, Japan, Indonesia and Italy.
  • Two more Indian dishes made the cut: Chicken 65 at No. 32 and papdi (papri) chaat at No. 40, from a list topped by South Korea's chikin, Indonesia's bator and Peru's jalea.
  • The dish traces its lineage to Persian and Central Asian kofta traditions of pounded meat, reshaped through Mughal-era cooking into the paneer-and-potato dumpling in creamy gravy served at Indian restaurants today.
  • Chef's rules for restaurant-style kofta at home: keep the potatoes dry, grate the paneer finely, use very little cornflour, fry at the right temperature — and never let the koftas sit in the gravy until serving.

Malai kofta — the crisp-on-the-outside, melting-on-the-inside dumpling that anchors North Indian restaurant menus — has been ranked the 10th best deep-fried dish in the world by Taste Atlas, the crowd-sourced food guide.

The ranking puts the vegetarian classic in the global top 10 of a 50-dish list led by South Korea's chikin at No. 1, followed by Indonesia's bator and Peru's jalea, and ahead of Japan's karaage at No. 8. Two more Indian dishes made the list: the fiery South Indian Chicken 65 at No. 32 and the street-food staple papdi chaat at No. 40.

Context & Background

Behind the familiar restaurant appeal is a dish with a long migration history. "The kofta has roots in Persian and Central Asian culinary traditions, where it was traditionally made with pounded or minced meat," Chef Ishijyot Surri, executive chef and founder of Mulk & SJI Hospitality, told the Indian Express. As those influences entered the subcontinent and fused with Mughal-era cooking, the kofta took on an Indian identity — adapted over generations to paneer, potato and vegetables, paired with rich, aromatic gravies.

"The kofta has roots in Persian and Central Asian culinary traditions, where it was traditionally made with pounded or minced meat."

— Chef Ishijyot Surri, Mulk & SJI Hospitality

What sets malai kofta apart, the chef says, is its contrast of textures: crisp outside, almost melting within, surrounded by a silky gravy. Unlike many classic Indian dishes that get their richness from ghee, malai kofta builds its body from a cashew-and-cream base.

Impact & Analysis

The No. 10 rank is another marker of Indian vegetarian cooking's growing global standing, in a list otherwise dominated by meat and seafood preparations — from Japan's katsu kare and ebi furai to Italy's fritto misto and Spain's croquetas. That a paneer dumpling outranks fried chicken entries from several countries says something about how far the cuisine has travelled beyond butter chicken and biryani in the world's imagination.

Taste Atlas rankings are compiled from its global community's ratings, and they have become a recurring fixture in food news — Indian dishes from butter chicken to Hyderabadi biryani have featured across its lists in recent years.

Diaspora Angle

For the diaspora, malai kofta is nostalgia plated: the safe vegetarian order at every restaurant table, the dish that anchors wedding buffets and Diwali spreads abroad. A global top-10 ranking gives Indian restaurants overseas one more reason to keep it on the menu — and gives home cooks a reason to attempt the chef's method rather than the shortcut.

What's Next

For readers attempting it at home, the chef's warnings are specific: use dry potatoes and minimal binding, or the koftas turn dense; fry at the wrong temperature and they fall apart; drown the dish in cream and the gravy turns heavy instead of silky. Cook the gravy base properly, blend and strain it, finish gently with kasuri methi and cardamom — and bring kofta and gravy together only at the last moment.
